text: About five hundred kilometres east of Mumbai, there's a hole in the ground almost two kilometres wide. It was made by a rock from space. And right now, the lake at its bottom is rising so fast that centuries-old temples are disappearing under the water. This is Lonar, one of the strangest places in India, and in this video you'll see why it's worth a trip this winter.

Lonar sits in Buldhana district, in the Vidarbha region of Maharashtra, on the flat volcanic tableland of the Deccan Plateau. From the road, you would never guess anything is here. The land is farms and scrub, almost perfectly flat. Then the ground simply drops away, and in front of you is a giant bowl, with a green lake at the bottom.

The crater is about one point eight kilometres across, and about one hundred and fifty metres deep. Its rim rises around twenty metres above the surrounding plain. The lake inside is roughly one point two kilometres wide. To picture the depth, a forty-storey tower standing on the crater floor would barely reach the rim.

So what made it? A meteorite. Estimates suggest a rock of about two million tonnes, travelling at roughly ninety thousand kilometres an hour. When it hit, it released energy often compared to a six megaton explosion, blasting out rock and throwing debris up to about two kilometres from the centre. Scientists later found shatter cones and shock-melted glass here, the fingerprints that only a hypervelocity impact leaves behind.

What makes Lonar special is the rock it hit. The Deccan Plateau is made of basalt, layers of lava that poured out around sixty-six million years ago. Lonar is often described as the only known impact crater on Earth formed entirely in basalt. That matters, because the surfaces of the Moon and Mars are also largely basalt. In twenty nineteen, an IIT Bombay study found minerals in Lonar's soil similar to those in rocks brought back by the Apollo missions. So scientists come here to study, on Earth, what impacts do on other worlds.

But how old is it? That's still being argued. Earlier thermoluminescence dating put the impact at about fifty-two thousand years ago. Then, in twenty eleven, argon dating suggested something ten times older, about five hundred and seventy thousand years. Some researchers think that older figure may be inflated by argon trapped in the rock. So the honest answer is somewhere between fifty thousand and about half a million years, and the debate isn't settled.

Local people have known this bowl for centuries. A British officer, C. J. E. Alexander, recorded it in eighteen twenty-three. For a long time, many thought it was an old volcano. Only later did geologists prove it was an impact crater. In nineteen seventy-nine, the Geological Survey of India declared it a National Geological Monument.

Now look at the water. Lonar lake has no outlet. Water comes in from rain and springs, but it can only leave by evaporating. Over thousands of years that has made the lake both salty and strongly alkaline, with a pH of about nine to ten and a half. Ordinary fish can't live in it, but microbes thrive. Several bacteria were first described to science from this lake, and some carry Lonar's name.

And in June twenty twenty, the lake did something nobody expected. In just two to three days, it turned from green to pink. Studies linked it to low water levels and higher salinity, which favoured salt-loving microbes rich in red and orange pigments. Photos went viral across India, and for a while, a crater in rural Maharashtra was national news.

People have treated this place as sacred for a very long time. Around the rim and on the lake shore are old stone temples, most dating from roughly the eleventh and twelfth centuries. The finest is the Daitya Sudan temple in Lonar town, built in the Hemadpanti style. Local legend says Vishnu killed a demon called Lonasura here, and that is where the name Lonar comes from. At the Gomukh temple on the crater edge, spring water flows constantly from a stone cow's mouth.

The crater is also protected for nature. It became part of the Lonar Wildlife Sanctuary, and in twenty twenty it was listed as a Ramsar wetland of international importance. Surveys have recorded about one hundred and sixty bird species, forty-six reptiles and twelve mammals in and around the crater. Monkeys, deer and migratory birds are common sights, especially in the cooler months.

But the biggest story at Lonar right now is the water itself. Over the last few years, the lake has been rising. In March twenty twenty-six, Maharashtra's forest minister told the state assembly it had risen by twenty to twenty-five feet. Other reports say fifteen to twenty feet. At least six temples near the shore have been submerged, including the Kamalja Devi temple, where water has entered the sanctum.

Why is it happening? Nobody is completely sure yet. Officials point to unusually heavy rain, and to four springs around the crater that keep flowing in. Because the lake has no outlet, every extra litre stays. In January twenty twenty-six, the Nagpur bench of the Bombay High Court ordered a public interest case on the rising water. IIT Bombay experts have been sampling the lake, and the state said it would seek wildlife permission to pump water out. Whether pumping is safe for such a unique lake is still being debated.

So why should you go? First, you can walk down into a crater made by a space rock, and stand on the shore of a lake it left behind. Second, the lake itself, salty, alkaline and home to life found almost nowhere else. Third, temples that are hundreds of years old, some of them now half underwater. And fourth, birds, forest and wide skies, just a day's drive from Mumbai.

Getting there is simple. The nearest airport is Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar, about one hundred and thirty-five to one hundred and forty kilometres away. The nearest railway stations are Jalna or Malkapur, each about ninety kilometres away. From any of them it's around two to three hours by taxi or state bus. The best time to go is October to March, when it's cool. From June to September, the trails get slippery.

One honest warning. The path down into the crater is steep and uneven, so carry water and go early. Some temples near the shore may be closed or underwater, so check locally before you go. And remember this is a protected and fragile lake. Don't litter, and don't touch or take anything from the water.
Should Maharashtra pump water out of Lonar to save the temples, or leave the lake to nature? Tell me in the comments. And if you like seeing places at their true scale, subscribe to True Scale.
